title: When is a caesarean section an option?
intro: A caesarean section is an operation in which a baby is born through a cut in the mother's abdomen and womb. It may be planned in advance or done in an emergency when vaginal birth is unsafe. It is also an option for some women who prefer it after discussion with their doctors.

sections.heading: Medical reasons for a planned caesarean
paragraphs: Reasons include the baby lying feet first or across in late pregnancy if turning has not worked, a placenta covering the cervix, certain infections such as high HIV viral load, previous complicated uterine surgery, severe maternal conditions and multiple pregnancies where the first baby is not head down. Doctors weigh the risks and benefits.

sections.heading: Emergency caesarean
paragraphs: It is done when labour does not progress, when the baby shows signs of distress, when there is heavy bleeding, a cord problem or concerns about the mother's health. Decisions are made quickly, usually under spinal anaesthetic or general anaesthetic if urgent.

sections.heading: Maternal request
paragraphs: Some women ask for a caesarean without a medical reason, for example because of fear of childbirth. Doctors should discuss the reasons, offer counselling and explain risks and benefits for mother and baby. Many guidelines say this request can be accepted after counselling. Planning a caesarean after a previous one is also possible, as is trying vaginal birth after caesarean for many women.

sections.heading: Risks and recovery
paragraphs: Compared with vaginal birth, caesarean is associated with more risk of infection, bleeding, blood clots and longer recovery, and with possible complications in future pregnancies, such as problems with the placenta. Recovery takes several weeks, with pain relief, gentle walking and support with lifting. Babies may have more breathing problems if born before thirty-nine weeks.

sections.heading: Making a decision
paragraphs: Ask about the reasons, alternatives, risks for you and your baby, timing and what to expect. Include your partner or support person. A second opinion or conversation with a midwife can help. You can change your mind, and decisions should respect your values.

examples.title: Preparing questions
examples.text: Imagine your baby is in breech position. You could ask about turning the baby, the risks of each option and the best timing.

examples.title: Planning recovery
examples.text: Suppose a planned caesarean is booked. You might arrange help at home and ask about pain relief and when you can drive.
